course.title: Shoemaking
course.tagline: Make sandals, slippers and shoes by hand, from cutting leather to a finished pair.

days.title: Shoemaking Tools and Materials
days.goal: Identify lasts, leather, soles and every hand tool a shoemaker needs.

video.title: How to Make Simple Sneakers

steps: Lay out a last (the foot-shaped form you build the shoe around), leather pieces, sole material, awl, hammer, knife and thread.
Feel the difference between upper leather, lining leather and sole leather.
Learn the shoe part names: vamp (front top), quarter (side), insole (inside bottom) and outsole (bottom).
Set up a clean, flat workbench with good light.
days.task: Label a diagram of a shoe with vamp, quarter, insole, outsole and heel.
days.challenge: Name every part of a shoe from memory, pointing at a real shoe.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a simple sneaker?
quiz.explain: Every shoe starts with measurements and a pattern for the upper.

quiz.q: What is a last?
options: A foot-shaped form shoes are built around
quiz.explain: The last gives the shoe its shape and size during making.

quiz.q: Why work with the shoe on the last?
options: It holds the shape while you stitch and glue
quiz.explain: The last keeps the upper in the correct three-dimensional shape.

days.title: Measure Feet Correctly
days.goal: Measure foot length, width and girth accurately for a good fit.

video.title: How to Make Simple Sneakers

steps: Trace both feet on paper while standing with weight on them.
Measure the length from heel to longest toe in centimetres.
Measure the width across the ball and the girth around the instep.
Compare left and right feet and note any difference.
days.task: Complete a foot measurement sheet for yourself and one other person.
days.challenge: Measure a foot in under three minutes with repeatable results.

days.title: Choose the Right Last
days.goal: Pick or adapt a last that matches the foot shape you measured.

video.title: How to Make Simple Sneakers

steps: Compare your foot measurements with the last length and width.
Check the last toe shape: round, square or pointed.
Note where the last is wider or narrower than the foot.
Pad a last with tape where extra width is needed.
days.task: Select the correct last size for a measured foot and explain why.
days.challenge: Adapt a last with tape to fit a wide foot.

days.title: Leather Basics: Types and Cuts
days.goal: Tell full-grain, top-grain and suede apart and cut leather on the right grain.

video.title: How to Measure Feet for Shoemaking

steps: Handle three leather types and note stretch, thickness and finish.
Find the tightest, least stretchy direction of a hide.
Cut a test strip along the backbone line where leather is strongest.
Thin a leather edge with a knife on a cutting board (thinning an edge like this is called skiving).
days.task: Cut four upper pieces from leather, all on the correct grain.
days.challenge: Skive a leather edge to half thickness without cutting through.

quiz.q: Why measure both feet standing up?
quiz.explain: Feet lengthen and widen under body weight, so standing measurements give the true fit.

quiz.q: Which measurement decides shoe length?
quiz.explain: Length comes from heel to the longest toe, usually the big or second toe.

quiz.q: Why measure the ball width?
options: So the shoe is wide enough where the foot bends
quiz.explain: The ball is the widest part and where the foot flexes when walking.

days.title: Pattern a Simple Sandal
days.goal: Draft a sandal upper pattern from a foot tracing.

video.title: How to Measure Feet for Shoemaking

steps: Trace the foot and draw the sandal outline 5mm outside the tracing.
Design two straps: one over the toes, one around the ankle.
Add 8mm seam allowance where straps join the sole.
Cut the pattern in paper and test it against the foot.
days.task: Draft and cut a paper pattern for a two-strap sandal.
days.challenge: Draft a sandal pattern for a child's foot from one tracing.

quiz.q: Why measure both feet standing up?

quiz.q: Which measurement decides shoe length?
quiz.explain: Length comes from heel to the longest toe, usually the big or second toe.

quiz.q: Why measure the ball width?
options: So the shoe is wide enough where the foot bends
quiz.explain: The ball is the widest part and where the foot flexes when walking.

days.title: Cut Uppers and Linings
days.goal: Cut leather uppers and linings cleanly and in matching pairs.

video.title: How to Measure Feet for Shoemaking

steps: Place the pattern on the leather avoiding scars and thin spots.
Cut with a sharp knife in one smooth motion, not sawing.
Cut the lining pieces slightly smaller than the uppers.
Mark left and right pieces so they never get mixed up.
days.task: Cut a matching pair of uppers and linings for sandals.
days.challenge: Cut a pair of uppers using the least leather possible.

days.title: Project: Make a Pair of Leather Slippers
days.goal: Assemble a simple pair of leather slippers from cut pieces to finished pair.

video.title: Harry Rogers Easy Shoemaking Series Part 1

steps: Glue the lining to the upper, then stitch the edges.
Attach the upper to the insole with contact adhesive.
Glue and press the outsole, then trim the edges flush.
Rub the sole edges with beeswax until smooth and shiny (this is called burnishing) and try the slippers on.
days.task: Finish a wearable pair of leather slippers.
days.challenge: Make the slippers with no glue showing at any edge.

quiz.q: What is a last in shoemaking?
options: A foot-shaped form you build the shoe around
quiz.explain: The last gives the shoe its shape and size while you work.

quiz.q: Why order the right lasts before you start your first shoe?
options: So the shoe is built to the right size and shape from the start
quiz.explain: Starting with the right last means the finished shoe fits the foot it was made for.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check when you start your first shoe?
options: That your last matches your foot measurements
quiz.explain: If the last does not match the foot, the shoe will not fit no matter how well you sew.

project.title: Make a Pair of Leather Slippers
project.brief: Assemble simple leather slippers from cut pieces to a finished, wearable pair.
checks: Uppers and linings cut in pairs

days.title: Stitching Leather by Hand
days.goal: Saddle stitch leather strongly with two needles and waxed thread.

video.title: Harry Rogers Easy Shoemaking Series Part 1

steps: Thread two needles on one length of waxed thread.
Punch stitch holes evenly with an awl or pricking iron.
Pass both needles through each hole in opposite directions.
Pull each stitch tight and keep the tension even.
days.task: Sew a 15cm leather seam with a saddle stitch (two needles passing through each hole in turn) and keep the stitches even.
days.challenge: Stitch a curved leather edge without puckering.

days.title: Lasting: Pulling Uppers Over the Last
days.goal: Last an upper onto the last so it takes the shoe shape.

video.title: Harry Rogers Easy Shoemaking Series Part 1

steps: Centre the upper on the last and tack it at the toe.
Pull the leather tight over the last with lasting pliers.
Fold the extra leather around the bottom (called the lasting allowance) under the insole and tack it there, working toe to heel.
Check the upper sits smooth with no wrinkles at the vamp.
days.task: Last one sandal upper smoothly onto a last.
days.challenge: Last an upper with no wrinkles at the toe.

days.title: Soles: Cutting and Shaping
days.goal: Cut, shape and finish outsoles and midsoles to match the last.

video.title: How to Make a Tabi Shoe Pattern

steps: Trace the lasted shoe onto sole leather or rubber sheet.
Cut the outsole 2mm proud of the upper all round.
Cut the sole edge at a slant (called bevelling) with a knife at 45 degrees.
Sand the sole edge smooth with coarse then fine sandpaper.
days.task: Cut and shape a pair of outsoles to match a lasted pair.
days.challenge: Shape a sole edge perfectly even all round.

quiz.q: How do you make a pattern from a last?
options: Wrap it in tape, draw design lines, cut the tape off and flatten it
quiz.explain: The tape-shell method captures the last's curves as a flat pattern.

quiz.q: What is a tabi shoe?
options: A shoe with a split toe
quiz.explain: Tabi shoes split the big toe from the rest, a traditional Japanese shape.

quiz.q: Why add seam allowance to a shoe pattern?
options: So pieces can be joined without shrinking the shoe
quiz.explain: Seam allowance is the extra material used to join pieces together.

days.title: Gluing and Attaching Soles
days.goal: Bond soles permanently with contact adhesive and correct pressing.

video.title: How to Make a Tabi Shoe Pattern

steps: Roughen both bonding surfaces with sandpaper.
Apply a thin even coat of contact adhesive to both sides.
Wait until the glue is tacky and dry to the touch.
Press the sole on firmly, then hammer the bond all round.
days.task: Glue a pair of soles that cannot be peeled off by hand.
days.challenge: Glue a sole with no squeeze-out visible at the edge.

days.title: Heels and Edge Finishing
days.goal: Build a stacked heel and burnish all edges to a clean finish.

video.title: How to Make a Tabi Shoe Pattern

steps: Cut three heel layers and glue them into a stack.
Shape the heel with a knife and sandpaper to match the sole.
Dampen the leather edges and rub them with beeswax and a smooth bone tool until shiny.
Polish the finished edges until they shine.
days.task: Build and attach a heel, then burnish all edges.
days.challenge: Burnish a sole edge to a glass-smooth shine.

days.title: Straps, Buckles and Closures
days.goal: Fit straps, buckles and Velcro closures that hold and adjust well.

video.title: How to Make Tabi Shoes

steps: Cut a strap to length allowing 3cm for the buckle fold.
Punch buckle holes evenly spaced 2cm apart.
Rivet or stitch a buckle securely to the strap.
Test the closure: it should hold firmly and release easily.
days.task: Fit a working buckle closure on a sandal strap.
days.challenge: Fit a strap that adjusts across three sizes.

quiz.q: What is saddle stitching?
options: Hand stitching with two needles passing through each hole
quiz.explain: Saddle stitch uses two needles and waxed thread for the strongest hand seam.

quiz.q: Why use waxed thread for leather?
options: It grips, resists rot and locks the stitch
quiz.explain: Wax helps the thread hold tension and protects it from moisture and wear.

quiz.q: What tool makes even stitch holes in leather?
quiz.explain: An awl or pricking iron punches evenly spaced holes for neat stitching.

days.title: Project: Make a Pair of Leather Sandals
days.goal: Make a complete pair of leather sandals with straps, soles and finished edges.

video.title: How to Make Tabi Shoes

steps: Cut uppers, linings and soles from your patterns.
Stitch and assemble the uppers, then last them.
Attach soles and heels, then burnish every edge.
Fit the sandals on the wearer and adjust the straps.
days.task: Finish a wearable pair of leather sandals.
days.challenge: Make sandals a customer would pay for at a market stall.

days.title: Sneaker Construction Basics
days.goal: Understand sneaker parts: foxing, toe cap, collar and cupsole.

video.title: How to Make Tabi Shoes

steps: Take apart an old sneaker and label each part.
Note how the upper is stitched to the middle sole layer (called the midsole).
Trace the cup sole — the rubber sole shaped like a cup that hugs the bottom of the shoe — and see how it wraps the upper.
Plan a simple sneaker upper in two panels.
days.task: Label every part of a dissected sneaker.
days.challenge: Sketch a two-panel sneaker upper that could be cut and sewn.

days.title: Pattern a Closed Shoe
days.goal: Draft a pattern for a closed shoe from a last and foot measurements.

video.title: How to Make Victorian Ballet Flats

steps: Wrap the last in masking tape and draw the design lines on it.
Cut the tape shell off and flatten it into a pattern.
Add seam allowances and mark the vamp and quarter lines.
Test the paper pattern by folding it back onto the last.
days.task: Draft a flattened tape pattern for a closed shoe.
days.challenge: Draft a pattern where the vamp and quarters meet cleanly.

quiz.q: What is a ballet flat made from?
options: A soft one-piece upper with a flexible sole
quiz.explain: Ballet flats use a soft upper gathered at the top with a thin flexible sole.

quiz.q: How does elastic keep a flat on the foot?
options: It gathers the top line so it hugs the foot
quiz.explain: Elastic around the top line pulls the opening snug around the foot.

quiz.q: Why is a soft shoe good for a beginner project?
options: It has few parts and teaches cutting, gathering and sole work
quiz.explain: A flat teaches the core skills with a simple one-piece pattern.

days.title: Sewing a Closed Upper
days.goal: Sew a closed shoe upper with strong seams and a neat lining.

video.title: How to Make Victorian Ballet Flats

steps: Stitch the vamp to the quarters with a saddle stitch.
Sew the back seam and press it flat.
Attach the lining, leaving the top edge open.
Turn the upper right side out and check the seams.
days.task: Sew a complete closed upper, lined and turned.
days.challenge: Sew an upper with no twisted seams.

days.title: Tabi and Shaped Shoes
days.goal: Make a shaped shoe like a tabi with a split toe.

video.title: How to Make Victorian Ballet Flats

steps: Study the tabi shape: a split between big toe and the rest.
Cut the split-toe pattern with extra allowance at the split.
Stitch the split carefully so it lies flat.
Last the tabi upper and check the toe shape holds.
days.task: Make one tabi-style shoe upper with a clean split toe.
days.challenge: Make a split toe that is comfortable to wear.

days.title: Ballet Flats and Soft Shoes
days.goal: Make a soft flat shoe with a gathered top line and elastic.

video.title: I Made Shoes! Beginner Shoemaking Tips and Tools

steps: Cut a one-piece upper for a ballet flat.
Gather the top line with elastic so it hugs the foot.
Attach a thin flexible sole.
Fit the flat and check it stays on when walking.
days.task: Make one soft ballet flat that stays on the foot.
days.challenge: Make a pair of flats that fold flat for travel.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of shoemaking for beginners?
options: Start simple and learn the tools before complex shoes
quiz.explain: Simple projects build tool skills and confidence before complex shoes.

quiz.q: Which tool cuts leather cleanly?
options: A sharp knife in one smooth cut
quiz.explain: A sharp knife cuts leather cleanly; sawing tears the edge.

quiz.q: Why keep leather away from scars and thin spots?
options: Weak spots tear and wear out fast
quiz.explain: Scars and thin areas are weak points that fail in a worn shoe.

days.title: Dyeing and Colouring Leather
days.goal: Dye leather evenly and seal it so the colour lasts.

video.title: I Made Shoes! Beginner Shoemaking Tips and Tools

steps: Clean the leather with a damp cloth and let it dry.
Apply dye in thin coats with a wool dauber, not one heavy coat.
Let each coat dry fully before the next.
Seal with a leather finish and buff to a shine.
days.task: Dye a leather sample evenly with no streaks.
days.challenge: Dye a pair of uppers one solid colour with no patchiness.

steps: Cut and sew both uppers with linings.
Last both shoes and attach insoles.
Glue soles and heels, then finish every edge.
Fit both shoes and photograph the finished pair.

days.challenge: Make closed shoes with matching left and right shaping.

days.title: Repair and Resoling
days.goal: Resole a worn shoe and repair a torn upper.

video.title: How to Make Leather Sandals by Hand

steps: Remove a worn outsole without damaging the upper.
Clean the old glue and roughen the surface.
Glue a new sole and trim it to the upper.
Stitch a torn upper seam and blend the repair.
days.task: Resole one worn shoe so it looks and feels new.
days.challenge: Repair a torn strap so the fix is invisible.

quiz.q: What are leather sandals usually made from?
options: Cut leather uppers, straps and a leather or rubber sole
quiz.explain: Handmade sandals combine leather uppers and straps with a shaped sole.

quiz.q: Why burnish sole edges?
options: To seal, smooth and strengthen the edge
quiz.explain: Burnishing compresses and seals the edge so it resists wear and looks finished.

quiz.q: What holds a sandal sole to the upper?
options: Contact adhesive plus stitching or tacks
quiz.explain: Contact adhesive bonds the sole, with stitching or tacks adding strength.

days.title: Comfort and Fit Testing
days.goal: Test fit properly: walking, standing and all-day comfort.

video.title: How to Make Leather Sandals by Hand

steps: Walk 100 steps in the shoes and note any rubbing.
Check the heel does not slip when walking.
Press the toe area: there should be 1cm of room.
Adjust straps or padding where rubbing occurs.
days.task: Fit-test a pair for comfort and record every fix needed.
days.challenge: Fix a heel-slip problem with padding, not a smaller size.

Attach the upper and test the clog for balance.
days.task: Make one clog with a shaped sole and secure upper.

days.title: Pricing and Selling Footwear
days.goal: Price handmade shoes from materials, time and a fair profit.

video.title: Handmade Leather Sandals Tutorial

steps: Add up leather, soles, thread and glue for one pair.
Time the build and value your hours fairly.
Add profit and compare with market prices for handmade shoes.
Write a simple price list for slippers, sandals and shoes.
days.task: Produce a price list for three shoe types with costs shown.
days.challenge: Price a custom pair for a named customer.

quiz.q: What is a clog sole made from?
options: Wood or cork shaped to the foot
quiz.explain: Clogs use a rigid shaped sole, traditionally wood, now often cork.

quiz.q: Why must a clog sole be level?
options: So it does not rock and the wearer walks safely
quiz.explain: A rocking sole is unstable and uncomfortable to walk on.

quiz.q: How is an upper fixed to a clog sole?
options: With tacks, nails or a stitched welt into the sole
quiz.explain: Uppers are mechanically fixed into the rigid sole so they cannot pull off.

video.title: Handmade Leather Sandals Tutorial

steps: Brush off dust, then apply cream polish in small circles.
Buff with a soft cloth until the shine is even.
Stuff the shoes with tissue to hold their shape.
Box or wrap the pair with a care card.
days.task: Present a finished pair polished, stuffed and boxed.
days.challenge: Polish a scuffed pair back to a shop shine.

Shoot from four angles: front, side, back and sole.
Use a plain background so the shoe stands out.

options: With tacks, nails or a stitched welt into the sole
quiz.explain: Uppers are mechanically fixed into the rigid sole so they cannot pull off.

video.title: How to Make Clog Sandal Soles

steps: Measure the client’s feet and write the numbers on an order sheet.
Agree the shoe type, leather and colour with the client.
Agree the price, deposit and delivery date in writing.
Keep the order sheet safe and follow it when you build.

quiz.q: Why photograph shoes from four angles?
options: So a buyer can judge shape, stitching and finish

quiz.q: What should a costing sheet include?
options: Materials, time, profit and selling price
quiz.explain: A real price comes from materials plus time plus profit.

quiz.q: Why stuff finished shoes with tissue?
options: To hold their shape in storage and display
quiz.explain: Tissue stuffing stops the uppers collapsing and creasing.

capstone.title: Make a Complete Pair of Shoes
capstone.brief: Design and build a complete pair of shoes of your choice (sandals, closed shoes or sneakers) for a real wearer, fitted, finished and presented with a costing sheet.
checks: Pair designed from a real foot measurement
Uppers cut, stitched and lasted cleanly
Soles and heels attached firmly with finished edges
Pair fits the wearer in length, width and comfort
Leather dyed or finished evenly if coloured
Costing sheet shows materials, time and selling price
deliverables: Finished pair of shoes, fitted and wearable
Foot measurement sheet for the wearer
Four photos: front, side, back and sole
